summary.text: At \(n=473165\), the odd number \(K=5292270077783=a(n)+4\) lies strictly between the two proposed endpoints.  The primes \(\{3,5,7,17,97,257,673\}\) form a period-\(48\) covering for \(K\): each satisfies \(2^{48}\equiv1\pmod p\), and checking the \(48\) exponent residues shows that some such prime properly divides \(K2^m+1\) for every \(m>0\), so \(K\) is itself a Sierpiński number.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=9454129+11184810n.
\]
Recall that a natural number \(k\) is a Sierpiński number here if it is odd, is greater than \(1\), and, for every positive integer \(m\), the number
\[
k2^m+1
\]
is not prime.

We disprove the assertion by giving one particular index for which there is another Sierpiński number strictly between the two alleged consecutive ones.

Take
\[
n=473165.
\]
A direct calculation gives
\[
11184810\cdot473165=5292260623650,
\]
and hence
\[
a(473165)=9454129+5292260623650=5292270077779.
\]
Define
\[
K=5292270077783=a(473165)+4.
\]
Then
\[
a(473165)=5292270077779<K=5292270077783

a(473165)+28=5292270077807,
\]
so
\[
a(473165)<K<a(473165)+28.
\]
It remains to prove that \(K\) is a Sierpiński number.

First, \(K\) is odd: explicitly,
\[
K=2\cdot2646135038891+1.
\]
It is also plainly greater than \(1\). We now show that \(K2^m+1\) is not prime for every positive integer \(m\). The divisors will come from the finite set
\[
\{3,5,7,17,97,257,673\}.
\]
The divisibility pattern is periodic in the exponent with period \(48\). We spell out the entire covering argument.

The relevant residues of \(K\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
p&3&5&7&17&97&257&673\\ \hline
K\bmod p&2&3&3&8&94&8&665.
\end{array}
\]
Thus these residues may also be written as
\[
K\equiv-1\pmod3,
\quad K\equiv3\pmod5,
\quad K\equiv3\pmod7,
\quad K\equiv8\pmod{17},
\]
\[
K\equiv-3\pmod{97},
\quad K\equiv8\pmod{257},
\quad K\equiv-8\pmod{673}.
\]
For the powers of \(2\), we use the following elementary congruences:
\[
2^2\equiv1\pmod3,
\quad 2^4\equiv1\pmod5,
\quad 2^3\equiv1\pmod7,
\quad 2^8\equiv1\pmod{17},
\]
\[
2^{48}\equiv1\pmod{97},
\quad 2^{16}\equiv1\pmod{257},
\quad 2^{48}\equiv1\pmod{673}.
\]
These are direct modular computations. For example, the period-\(48\) statements can also be checked from
\[
2^{48}-1=281474976710655,
\]
which is divisible by both \(97\) and \(673\) (indeed, the respective quotients are \(2901803883615\) and \(418239192735\)). The smaller-period identities follow immediately from
\(2^2=4\), \(2^4=16\), \(2^3=8\), \(2^8=256\), and \(2^{16}=65536\), reduced modulo the indicated numbers.

We now cover every possible exponent \(m\) according to its residue modulo \(48\).

1. Suppose \(m\) is even. Since \(2^2\equiv1\pmod3\), we have \(2^m\equiv1\pmod3\). Since \(K\equiv-1\pmod3\),
\[
K2^m+1\equiv(-1)(1)+1\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
Thus \(3\mid K2^m+1\).

2. It remains to consider odd \(m\). If \(m\equiv3\pmod4\), then \(2^m\equiv2^3\equiv8\equiv3\pmod5\). Since \(K\equiv3\pmod5\),
\[
K2^m+1\equiv3\cdot3+1=10\equiv0\pmod5.
\]
Thus \(5\mid K2^m+1\).

3. The odd exponents not covered by the preceding case satisfy \(m\equiv1\pmod4\). If in fact \(m\equiv1\pmod8\), then \(2^m\equiv2\pmod{17}\), because \(2^8\equiv1\pmod{17}\). As \(K\equiv8\pmod{17}\),
\[
K2^m+1\equiv8\cdot2+1=17\equiv0\pmod{17}.
\]
Thus \(17\mid K2^m+1\).

4. The only exponents not yet covered satisfy \(m\equiv5\pmod8\). Modulo \(48\), these are precisely the six residue classes
\[
5,13,21,29,37,45.
\]
We treat all six.

If
\[
m\equiv5,21,\text{ or }37\pmod{48},
\]
then in every case \(m\equiv5\pmod{16}\). Since \(2^{16}\equiv1\pmod{257}\),
\[
2^m\equiv2^5=32\pmod{257}.
\]
Together with \(K\equiv8\pmod{257}\), this gives
\[
K2^m+1\equiv8\cdot32+1=257\equiv0\pmod{257}.
\]
Hence \(257\mid K2^m+1\) in these three residue classes.

If \(m\equiv13\pmod{48}\), then \(m\equiv1\pmod3\). Since \(2^3\equiv1\pmod7\), we get \(2^m\equiv2\pmod7\). Since \(K\equiv3\pmod7\),
\[
K2^m+1\equiv3\cdot2+1=7\equiv0\pmod7.
\]
Thus \(7\mid K2^m+1\).

If \(m\equiv29\pmod{48}\), the period-\(48\) congruence modulo \(97\) gives
\[
2^m\equiv2^{29}\equiv65\pmod{97}.
\]
For completeness, the last residue follows by repeated squaring: modulo \(97\),
\[
2^4=16,
\quad 2^8\equiv256\equiv62,
\quad 2^{16}\equiv62^2\equiv61,
\]
and multiplying the powers corresponding to \(29=16+8+4+1\) gives \(2^{29}\equiv65\pmod{97}\). As \(K\equiv-3\pmod{97}\),
\[
K2^m+1\equiv(-3)\cdot65+1=-194=-2\cdot97\equiv0\pmod{97}.
\]
Therefore \(97\mid K2^m+1\).

Finally, if \(m\equiv45\pmod{48}\), then
\[
2^m\equiv2^{45}\equiv589\equiv-84\pmod{673}.
\]
One direct repeated-squaring check is
\[
2^8\equiv256,
\quad 2^{16}\equiv255,
\quad 2^{32}\equiv417\pmod{673},
\]
and multiplication according to \(45=32+8+4+1\) gives \(2^{45}\equiv589\pmod{673}\). Since \(K\equiv-8\pmod{673}\),
\[
K2^m+1\equiv(-8)(-84)+1=672+1=673\equiv0\pmod{673}.
\]
Thus \(673\mid K2^m+1\).

This exhausts all possibilities: every integer is either even or odd; an odd exponent is either \(3\pmod4\) or \(1\pmod4\); one that is \(1\pmod4\) is either \(1\pmod8\) or \(5\pmod8\); and the latter class splits modulo \(48\) into exactly \(5,13,21,29,37,45\). Consequently, for every positive integer \(m\), at least one number in
\[
\{3,5,7,17,97,257,673\}
\]
divides \(K2^m+1\).

This divisor is always nontrivial. Every number in the covering set is at least \(3\) and at most \(673\), while
\[
K2^m+1>K>673.
\]
Thus the divisor is greater than \(1\) and strictly smaller than \(K2^m+1\). A prime number has no such divisor, so \(K2^m+1\) is not prime. This holds for every positive \(m\). Together with the facts that \(K\) is odd and \(K>1\), it proves that \(K=5292270077783\) is a Sierpiński number.

We have therefore found, at \(n=473165\), a Sierpiński number \(K\) satisfying
\[
a(473165)<K<a(473165)+28.
\]
Hence \(a(473165)\) and \(a(473165)+28\) cannot be consecutive Sierpiński numbers. The assertion that this happens for every \(n\ge0\) is false.
